Back when Counter-Strike tried a campaign mode. 

The game is a series of mini-objectives against bots on various maps, while the Deleted Scenes extra is a full blown CS campaign with many elements of the online game being brought in with solo FPS gameplay mechanics (such as equipment) to make a fun and hilarious game (the stereotypical russian accents make me laugh every time). 

The multiplayer part is quite similar to the original CS but with slightly better textures.

Overall, this isn't a game for people who like CS:GO, it's more for the fans of old school FPS games and OG Counter-Strikers. I do recommend it nonetheless, but keep in mind that the game is over 10 years old.

If you want to be destroyed by people who've been playing the game since CS 1.1 release and are tryhard mlg pros that wallbang headshot you with dualies from across the map, you get 1.6.

If you want to play dress up dolls with your guns, get scammed out of your skins, and play with a bunch of blokes in a matchmaking system that sometimes works but mostly queues you into a game consisting of anyone ranging from people who just installed the game to Global Elite smurfs with Silver IV accounts with ridiculous updates that make a $700 pistol the most powerful gun in the game,you get Global Offensive.

If you want to play a ton of surf, bhop, prison, scoutsknivez, and many more minigames and never find any servers with the actual core game, you get Source.

If you want to have fun, play with a decent community, use guns that are mostly not broken, have a game that can run on nearly any computer, and actually play the core Counter-Strike game, you get Condition Zero.

Counter Strike: Condition Zero comes with two games:
1. Condition Zero
2. Condition Zero: Deleted Scenes

1. Condition Zero
Basically Counter Strike 1.6 but with improved graphics and the addition of bots. The bots are amazing considering when this game was released (they're still inferior to human players). In addition, the bots are a great way for beginners to learn about the game in a more relaxed environment. There is also a singleplayer Tour of Duty, which is basically regular counter strike missions against bots, but with additional challenges (example: kill 3 enemies with a sniper rifle). Sadly, the Tour of Duty missions are Counter-Terrorist only. There are no Terrorist missions.

2. Condition Zero: Deleted Scenes
This is a singleplayer game. It uses the same weapons and game mechanics as Condition Zero, but with some additions, including the awsome fiber optic camera. Level design is one of Deleted Scenes' greatest strengths. The AI is passable. The story is where it fails, in that each mission is its own self-contained story with practically no connecting elements. I suspect you don't even play as the same person in each mission. Immersion takes a serious hit because of this. It helps to pretend you are playing as the same person. I recommend Adrian Shephard before Black Mesa.

I had a lot of fun playing Condition Zero and Deleted Scenes. I highly recommend these games as well as any other Counter Strike game (or any game by Valve for that matter). By the way, check out the first screenshot on the store page. Really take a close look at the plane...

With its extensive Tour of Duty campaign, a near-limitless number of skirmish modes, updates and new content for Counter-Strike's award-winning multiplayer game play, plus over 12 bonus single player missions, Counter-Strike: Condition Zero is a tremendous offering of single and multiplayer content.

Counter-Strike: Condition Zero is a follow up to the original Counter-Strike game. This game was released in 2004, so almost eleven years ago. Condition Zero uses the Half-Life engine. 

What we have here is a CS game which includes a single player mission pack. When it comes to playing Counter-Strike, I am more or less a newb at it. This game gave me the perfect opportunity to learn the guns, maps and mission types without the pressure of feeling like you are letting your team down by sucking. The campaign took me about four hours to complete, but this was only on Normal mode, you can go back and replay the missions on a higher difficulty to eventually work your way up to playing online. 

I also found the squad management system to be a nice little feature which isn't seen in other CS games, at the start of each mission, you can choose which squad members to take with you on the mission, each of the team members have their positive and negative stats so you can really get stuck in with min-maxing them. You start out with three members and you work you way up to having a full blown squad of about eight men. 

On each of the missions you also have to complete specific challenges, these can be goals set around killing a certain amount of people, winning the match in less than ninety seconds, rescuing a specific amount of hostages etc etc. This added a little variety of play, especially the challenges where you have to use a certain weapon in order to complete them. This allowed you to learn how to use other guns effectively rather than sticking with your tried and tested Rifle and Deagle. 

While the graphics do not come close to looking like games we have in the current day, the game still does look nice. I wasn't put off by the dated graphics one bit; I guess that just shows how good the Half Life engine actually is!  

The difficulty levels completely rely on how hard you want to make it. I started out on Normal mode just to get to grips with the game as I am newb like that; but you can work all the way up to playing as if you are in a match online and have the brutally hard experience if you want to. Easy mode is complete walk in the park though, enemies can be standing in front of you for about three seconds before they realize they should shoot you, and even then they spray bullets randomly all around you without actually hitting, so I wouldn't recommend you start out on Easy mode. 

Like I said, the campaign took me about four hours to complete, but there are two or three more difficulty levels to try out, and I can see this adding a lot of variety into the game play, so I can easily see the single player alone taking about twelve hours to complete it fully on all difficulties. 

I found no technical issues what so ever while playing, I would assume all the bugs and niggles would of been ironed out years ago.. 

In conclusion I can easily recommend Counter-Strike: Condition Zero for anyone looking to get into the FPS or CS scene, it will easily give you a worthwhile experience, giving you the opportunity to learn all of the CS maps, guns and game modes in a pressure free environment.

I'll be clear immediately: I'm a very casual fan of this series. I really don't care for Counter-Strike 2, how it outright replaced CSGO, how it essentially killed CSGO's casual content (all custom and most official), and its seemingly even further hardlined esports direction. I don't exactly enjoy the playerbase """communication""" in this series either, so there's basically no incentive for me to bother at this point.

So then, somehow, Condition Zero has stood the test of time even though infamously nobody cared about it. It stands up just because it simply has by far the best singleplayer offerings in the series. This is the only entry to have an Unreal Tournament style singleplayer (Tour of Duty) where you'll be given a checklist of normal bot matches with multiple challenges to complete in order to win per match. The bots could be better (it should be noted though the bots use "voice chat" to communicate what they're doing and planning, which you can also use chat commands to somewhat influence them too) but this mode turned out to be a very respectable way of keeping the series alive for me. There's a bunch of mission pack mods to extend the playtime of Tour of Duty too, so it massively adds value to Condition Zero.

Bizarrely too it contains a proper traditional singleplayer campaign via a series of singleplayer missions via "Deleted Scenes"; mildly comparable to Half-Life (only because Deleted Scenes plays much more like as if it's just another Half-Life expansion pack, rather than being true Counter-Strike). I'm not even going to pretend your time isn't probably much better spent on just playing the entire Half-Life collection or the Tour of Duty mode instead, but it does exist.

Of course there's multiplayer too, but nobody's playing it. It does seem to have benefited from HL1's anniversary update, so it doesn't look like it would take much to run a server for friends at least.

I recommend this one just for the fact it's the most reasonable game for singleplayer in the series, even if you don't care about Deleted Scenes.

Counter Strike Condition Zero is the sequel to the original Counter Strike and now it includes a Single Player Campaign, so let's take a look shall we ?

When I mentioned that this game has a single player campaign, I didn't mean a story mode. The single player campaign is a very short bundle of missions where you have few objectives during each missions. Like rescue hostages, defuse bombs and take out terrorists with a specific weapon.

The missions are incredibly short and you can finish all 12 within 2 hours. 

The AI will make the hostage missions a living hell. Once the round starts the AI are on the hunt to find any enemy player on the field and will not help you so don't expect any help from the AI. Getting a hostage to a drop off, before your team kills the entire enemy team.

The gameplay is not much different from the original Counter Strike so don't expect a major change.

Now for the feature everyone cares. THE MULTIPLAYER. It's almost completely dead. I had trouble finding a match and when I did get into a full lobby match, I felt bored and it's not as good as the original Counter Strike.

This game is not good, but it's not horrible either. The campaign is short and not worth the money and the multiplayer is slowly dying out. In the end only get this if you're a hardcore fan, otherwise get any other game in the franchise.

Counter-Strike: Condition Zero is an expansion pack and, in a sense, a visual upgrade for Counter-Strike 1.6, with more HD looking models and new detail textures, which were created for the game's exclusive maps for a better graphical experience, but there's more than meets the eye.

CS:CZ introduced a campaign mode, called the Tour of Duty, which is treated as a single-player experience, consisting of tasks that the player must complete if they want to advance to the next mission. The Tour of Duty campaign consists of 6 chapters, called "tours", with each tour containing 3 maps (missions) in it. In order to efficiently play against the enemy team and be able to have a chance on winning them, it is strongly recommended/most definitely essential that one recruits members for their team, though that comes with a cost. The amount/skill-strength of soldiers that the player is able to recruit is determined by Reputation Points, which are gained by completing missions (though some are also granted to the player at the beginning of the tour, and the amount depends on the difficulty chosen). In general the campaign is pretty easy to learn and while it can sometimes be frustrating due to either some ridiculous tasks (especially in harder difficulties) or just the difficulty of the game itself, it's still a fun and addictive experience.

Since CS:CZ is the first game that introduced built-in bots, the game also technically introduced an offline (multiplayer) mode, which gives the player the ability to either target practice or just kill some time, but everything else is identical to CS 1.6.

CS:CZ had received quite the undeserving flak because it was released in the same year as the Source engine, which was Valve's breakthrough product, and since with it also came Counter-Strike: Source, it's only natural that it would unfortunately outshine this game in every aspect and place it as an "obsolete on arrival" product. Also the fact that the development state of this game had been bad in every aspect, having changed development teams twice over the course of 4 years, which obviously brought over significant delay, very sadly helped in making Condition Zero lose most of its relevance by the time that it hit the shelves.

With everything being said above, CZ's infamous reputation among the Counter-Strike franchise is attributed not as much to it being "lackluster" as it is to it being unlucky due to all the delays, overhauls as well as the horrendously bad timing of its release with the Source engine. Otherwise, this game has much to offer and its status as an underrated cult-classic is here to stay.

The forgotten, underappreciated Counter Strike. If you loved playing with bots, you'll love Condition Zero. Bot AI is pretty damn good to the point where even the hostages have their own AI, being a lot more reactive and feeling more human to interact with. They'll try to escape on their own if unguarded, get scared if terrorists aim at them, wave to counter-terrorists if they see them and no terrorists are nearby, react to grenades (flash/smoke/frag), etc.

This is also the only Counter-Strike I know that comes with an actual singleplayer mode known as Deleted Scenes. It's janky as hell and very flawed, but I appreciate the effort nonetheless. Deleted Scenes would be better if it had mod support and if enemies dropped their weapons on death. For some inexplicable reason, you cannot pickup weapons from dead enemies in Deleted Scenes, even though that's always been a feature of every Counter Strike game.

Tour of Duty mode is my favorite even though I hate how completing challenges is mandatory. I just wish the Challenges weren't mandatory to complete in order to progress the Tour of Duty mode. The "bot roster" system in ToD mode is also cool, as you get to pick which bots to take with you. 

Maverick is my absolute favorite, as he's an absurdly cheap teammate (3 points) who happens to have High Skill. Normally, High Skill bots cost 4 or 5 points. Maverick is a High Skill bot who is available early on, but at the cost of being a loose cannon that disobeys orders. He's so endearing and memorable.

People often dunk on Condition Zero for being just a reskin of CS 1.6. They may be right at one point, but
people often overlook that CZ brought things that may not look like much, though given the amounts of small improvements combined together, it's quite lots.

but people either praise 1.6 for CZ's features or they never really even played CZ to experience it.

For example, maps and models in CZ have so much better visual clarity. I mean, sure, some maps look completely different, straying from the original, but they do help you differentiate between CT and T Models quite well... especially in darker corners of maps...

For a generation of gamers who grew up with unreliable dial-up internet, strict household screen-time rules, or computers that simply couldn't handle the jump to Source, Counter-Strike: Condition Zero was an absolute godsend. It is a beautifully unique piece of Valve history that transformed a hardcore, online-only multiplayer sweat-fest into a deeply comforting, accessible single-player experience. Firing it up today instantly triggers a wave of mid-2000s nostalgia, calling back to the days of tweaking bot difficulty sliders on a dusty Windows XP machine, all while the familiar, crunchy GoldSrc engine weapon sounds echoed through your headphones.

The heart and soul of this game lies in its iconic "Tour of Duty" campaign mode. Instead of getting instantly headshotted by online players who spent 14 hours a day practicing recoil patterns, Condition Zero gave you a tactical, progress-based ladder to climb at your own pace. You were tasked with building your own custom squad of AI counter-terrorists—each with their own funny dossiers, bravery stats, and favorite weapons—to take down bots across classic maps like de_dust2 and cs_militia. The addition of specific level challenges, like forcing you to get a certain number of kills with a tactical shield or a Grenade Launcher before moving on, turned standard CS matches into addictive, arcade-like puzzle levels.

Then, of course, there is the legendary Deleted Scenes campaign—a completely separate, linear single-player story that feels like an interactive 2004 action movie. Getting to play as specialized international forces, from the British SAS to the French GIGN, while sneaking through secret Siberian facilities or escaping a crashed helicopter, gave the rigid CS gunplay a wonderfully cinematic flavor. It represents a lost era of game development where developers weren't trying to sell you weapon skins or battle passes; they were just trying to give you a solid, offline campaign to blow through on a rainy Friday night. It remains a flawless, nostalgic comfort-food shooter that deserves a spot in every classic PC gaming library.

[b]Counter-Strike: Condition Zero[/b] is a game that could’ve been something more but ended up as an underwhelming entry in the Counter-Strike franchise. Released in 2004, this game is built on the same engine that powered Half-Life and the original Counter-Strike—both of which are revolutionary in their own right. However, Condition Zero fails to capture the same magic.

One of the most glaring issues is that despite the solid foundation of the GoldSrc engine, which worked wonders in Half-Life, Condition Zero somehow manages to feel like a downgrade. The single-player mode, which was supposed to be the big selling point with its “Tour of Duty” campaign and Deleted Scenes, feels like an awkward afterthought. The AI is laughably bad—your bot teammates either act like total beginners or morph into super soldiers with the reaction times of an aimbot. There's no in-between. And don’t even get me started on the dated graphics and clunky animations; it's like they didn't even try to update them from the original Counter-Strike.

The multiplayer, while still technically “Counter-Strike,” doesn’t really offer anything new. The maps, while slightly improved, don’t justify the game’s existence, especially when Counter-Strike 1.6 was still around and doing the same things better. Even worse, the game was released just months before Counter-Strike: Source, making it feel obsolete almost immediately.

While some players might find nostalgia in its simplicity or appreciate the minor updates in models and textures, it's hard to argue that Condition Zero was worth its full price tag when it dropped. It's a game that got lost in its own development hell, and by the time it was released, it was just too little, too late

This game came out at the wrong time and as a result has a bad reputation. If we rewind to when this game came out, you either had counter strike for free as a mod for half life, or you paid for a bundle that included half life and counter strike together. 

This game came around during that time. For many, it was not worth spending extra money on a game you already had. CS 1.6 was one of the most popular games around and had a huge active community. Condition Zero was not merged into CS 1.6 so this game had its own set of servers, however the gameplay was identical to CS 1.6. 

Fast forward 20 years. CS 1.6 is still active but the community is small, with most servers only running dust 2 or a zombie mod. CS-Source is dead. CS:GO has been phased out and replaced with CS2. From this perspective is where I find it most fair to review Condition Zero.

Condition Zero first and foremost has far better player models. They look fantastic compared to CS 1.6. The game includes all the original maps in 1.6 plus updated Condition Zero versions with better textures and improved layouts. Think of it like an HD textures pack for a 20+ year old game.

Unlike CS 1.6, this game includes bots with multiple difficulty levels. You do not have to deal with joining suspicious looking servers. You will find that if you try to play 1.6 online, those still left are very, very good at the game and it is not a fun experience. The bots give you a chance to play 1.6 again on a somewhat fair level. 

Performance wise, I have found this game runs great. In 1.6 on modern machines, the player models look like they are lagging/jagged and at times stuttering. Almost as if it is a clay-mation stop motion movie.  I play at 2560x1080 resolution and I can say without hesitation this version of the game looks far superior in motion than 1.6 

In a nutshell, this game should be best viewed as a re-master of CS 1.6 that came out 20 years too soon.

Counter-Strike:Condition Zero is an interesting one. At a glance, Condition Zero (CZ) looks similar to CS 1.6 but with better looking weapon and player models. However, the game actually has a few differences in terms of content.

There's the classic multiplayer mode that has official bot support for the maps that come with the game. This part of the game should be familiar to those who play CS 1.6. You can install new maps and the game will attempt to generate the navigation mesh for the bots. If the bots aren't playing well on custom maps, you can finetune it manually too.

There's also a Tour of Duty campaign mode where you are given "scenarios" that are using the multiplayer maps with specific victory conditions. Clearing scenarios gives you points, which you can use to recruit teammates who join your team as friendly bots. This mode is actually moddable as well, so you can create your own campaigns.

The bots can differ in their difficulty as well, which is kind of nice. Being older now (Man, has it been that long since CZ came out?), I always appreciate it when games have bot support. Sure, it can't replicate the experience of pitting your skills against real players but bots are great for warming up or for days where you just want to chill or mess around to relax.

Outside of multiplayer, there is a decent singleplayer campaign, called Deleted Scenes, that revolves around individual counter-terrorist scenarios, allowing you to play as the different CT units that are portrayed in multiplayer such as the SEALs, GSG9 and SAS. It's actually pretty fun, all things considered and it answers the question: "What if Counter-Strike had a singleplayer campaign?".

Despite being on the GoldSrc engine, there's just something about the pre-Source Counter-Strikes that I really like. Maybe its the nostalgia glasses here but I prefer the responsiveness of the GoldSrc engine to the floatiness that Source seems to have at times. And maybe its because I grew up during the GoldSrc era and I've gotten so used to the look of the game and the other GoldSrc games.

If there's another reason why I've stuck with CZ and CS 1.6, it might be because that unlike Global Offensive, one does not need to pay money for skins just to customise their game. One can go to dedicated modding sites to find weapon skins, player models and maps to enhance their Counter-Strike experience. However, do take note that because CS 1.6 is its predecessor, CZ has lesser mods available for it.

Overall, if you already have CS 1.6, CZ's multiplayer mode doesn't really add much but if you are interested in the singleplayer campaign, you could get CZ just for that.

A Nostalgic Journey with Some Hidden Gems

Alright, let’s talk about Counter-Strike: Condition Zero. I’m sure a lot of you probably know it’s the “odd one out” in the Counter-Strike series, sandwiched between the original and Source. And yeah, it’s got its flaws, but I can’t help but feel a sense of nostalgia whenever I load it up.

First off, this game has that classic Counter-Strike feel. If you’ve played 1.6, you’ll instantly feel at home. The core mechanics are there: team-based, tactical gameplay, bomb planting, hostage rescues, all that good stuff. There’s a reason CS became a staple in the FPS world, and Condition Zero carries that legacy well, even though it wasn’t as big as its predecessors.

Now, here's the thing about Condition Zero—it introduced a single-player component that was actually kind of fun. You get these little AI matches where you can practice your skills or just mess around. Sure, the bots aren’t the brightest, but they do provide a decent challenge if you’re looking to warm up or just want to play at your own pace without the pressure of online matches.

The real hidden gem here, though, is the Deleted Scenes campaign. It’s not perfect, but it was an interesting attempt to give Condition Zero a single-player story mode (something the franchise didn’t have before). You go through different missions that range from stealthy approaches to all-out gunfights. The voice acting is... well, let’s just say it’s not going to win any awards, but it’s got that goofy charm you can appreciate if you’re into retro FPS campaigns.

I won’t lie, the AI is a little clunky, and the missions can get repetitive, but there’s something oddly satisfying about taking on terrorists in a more structured way than the usual match-based chaos. For people who loved CS but wanted something different, Deleted Scenes was kind of an underappreciated bonus.

Now, let’s be real for a second. Condition Zero doesn’t hold up to Counter-Strike: Source or Global Offensive. It’s got that weird in-between vibe, where it’s not as polished or fluid as Source, and the graphics—while decent for its time—look pretty dated now. The bots can be hilarious (in a bad way), and the online community was smaller than in the CS 1.6 days, which made it tough to get a full, active match going.

Also, it had this weird mix of being too “arcade” for the hardcore competitive scene but not casual enough to be a proper “fun” game for people who just want to jump in and shoot stuff. It’s like Condition Zero didn’t really know what it wanted to be, and as a result, it kinda fell into this awkward middle ground that wasn’t as well-received by the wider community.

For me, though, Condition Zero is still a solid pick if you’re a fan of Counter-Strike. It may not be the top dog in the series, but it’s got that old-school charm. The maps feel classic, and the gunplay still holds up, even if it doesn’t have the same polish as its successors. Plus, if you’re into the history of Counter-Strike, this game is like a weird little snapshot of where the series was trying to go before Source changed everything.

If you’re into retro FPS games and enjoy diving deep into older titles that didn’t quite make it, Condition Zero is worth checking out. Just don’t expect it to dethrone CS 1.6 or Source.

It feels better, it looks better, it plays better. I would even dare to say it's like if 1.6 got a final 2.0 update. A good game that unfortunately was released way too late at a very bad time after a complicated development. It deserved much more attention and appreciation. It still does today. Take AI for example, in a moment I literally forgot I was playing a 2004 game because of how complex bots act on maps in a certain situations compared to many modern titles. Being the commander I can order teammates what strategy we choose while approaching and searching for the enemies. All the radio communications between the whole team is such a nice touch that gives you that special operation feeling you're in. That is the reason I had plenty of fun playing the Tour of Duty against the bots on quite interesting and unique maps, many of which I've never seen in any future game in that series.

Now let's talk about Deleted Scenes with which I fell in deep love with. I want to focus on that mode since it is the main reason this game stands out. To describe it as simple as possible, it feels like a good old MoH or CoD just without complex storyline, memorable characters and betrayals. Here we have 19 mid-length levels with one main objective, 6 of which are only available via World Map for some strange reason and one is a training which is usual for HL spin-offs. None of them are connected to each other and you just experience separate events and prevent the worst terroristic outcome as an operative of a given CT organization. It has its own charm and atmosphere, looks and action. It gives that amazing special agent feeling, like Splinter Cell does, but with a classic CS shooting and movement (which I honestly consider a great combination). There are plenty of stealth and explosive action almost each level you play. Some may say it is the same shooting range as CoD, which I might agree with at some degree, yet it still feels different. Yes, you're mostly a one man army (even though there are many times you fight alongside your teammates), but somehow I still feel like it's more tactical and mundane, if it makes any sense. I love how it goes around the world as you also play for different organizations and their respective operatives as if they were fighting together against one evil at the same time. Kinda giving me that Rainbow Six vibes.
I liked all of the levels, but I had an absolute blast playing Russian campaign, and considering it's surprising to see Spetsnaz in Counter-Strike game on its own already felt heartwarming and in some sense even heroic (play Secret War and you'll get what I mean). Sure, I might sound bias, but man, the Russians which are not portrayed as stereotypical bad guys but actual operatives which are fighting against terrorism for 3 separate levels in such a game? That's something I truly appreciate. The only thing that somehow annoyed me there was Hankagai level set in Japan. I loved every Japanese part of this campaign, but in that specific level I was struggling to find the right path of where I actually need to go to proceed further. I think I spent more time on it than 2 levels I played before combined. Sometimes you just have to go back where you came from, and sometimes you have to find some sort of a vent or a climbing structure that is not that obvious to spot. And then Miami Heat. Oh boy, there is something wrong with the starting sewer part of that one. Don't get me wrong, I quite enjoyed "puzzles" in the tradition of the original Half-Life, and I believe it actually diversifies the gameplay, making it not tedious and monotonous. But I was genuenly confused what else should I do to approach the next area which was blocked by a big immovable metal cube. At first I thought, since it was too heavy, I should probably make the water hit upper level to be able to move it forward (at least that's how I know an object can be moved a bit easier). And the hint for that seemed to be the same cube I was able to move just before entering the pipe with that blocking thing. But there was nothing helpful to rise the water level, as I already used all the valves. I kid you not, I spent good 20 minutes walking back all the areas I've been at, looking for something I missed. And then when my patience expired, I came back to that cube and started grabbing it in a different directions. Guess what happened when I started to spam different buttons? It actually moved. Belive it or not, the way I was able to do so was grabbing it with "E", holding it with "W" and then spamming "F" which is a toggle for night vision. Is there anything that can explain why does it work this way? Absolutely not and that's frustrating af. I actually decided to check YT for that mission and seems like I'm not the only one who got stuck there. The only difference is that it wasn't moving for me at all until I started mashing "F". But besides all that the rest of the level is pretty good.

It's pretty short, but hella fun and entertaining. And for those people who claim no one needs and cares about single player CS, that's where you mistaken a lot. You got your beloved not always fair PvP since 1999 which no one ever tried to take away from you (except CS:GO, but that's a different story now). But do you seriously want to push all that huge potential and the basis for the plot component of that series away just because it is most famous for its multiplayer? I understand that it's not very correct to give examples of a more modern while speaking about retro-ish games, but take Titanfall 2 for example, was it a bad idea to make a campaign for a sequel when the prequel never had it in the first place? I like Battlefield 3 for its single-player campaign and the emotions it conveys, did making it somehow take anything from the multiplayer? Both had enjoyable single player and a great multiplayer people still remember to this day. Or take Rainbow Six Siege (years 1-3), who wouldn't want to play a full-fledged campaign in that setting with those characters? And speaking of which, there was meant to be a campaign mode that sadly got cancelled. That would be awesome, and you know it if you ever played any single player Rainbow Six game. I'm gonna express a very controversial thought, but in my honest opinion Condition Zero Deleted Scenes is a more Counter-Strike than GO/2 could've ever become. The whole anti-terrorist fight for the better safe future feeling is there and I doubt any of the modern game can achieve the same level. The story is always appreciated and that's why a high percent of people prefer single player over a multiplayer with a not always necessary grind/overcoming. And considering the new operations (which was AT LEAST SOMETHING lore wise) are not coming to 2, it is even more valuable to try today.

You might be questioning, why I haven't said anything about the backbone of the series, the multiplayer itself. The thing is, as of today there are very little count of servers you can play on (such as a zombie mod), but I don't see many people play CZ. I haven't seen at least one server with more than 10 people at a time, even though steam shows ~200+ online. I guess those who wanted something from early 2000 picked 1.6 or Source for a more defined experience. Or maybe some servers are hidden for me, I don't know.

[h3] In conclusion: [/h3]
The multiplayer is mostly dead last time I checked. If you hop in on time, you may find a full server where you can have plenty of fun for a few hours.
The Tour of Duty is nice to give yourself a little bit of a challenge if you got used to play classic bomb/hostage mode. Just a bit tedious to my taste if you really want to get all 4 medals.
Deleted Scenes campaign is great! Ritual Entertainment has earned my respect. They did a magnificent job on it. Its length is around 6-8h but that's more than enough to get the joy and entertain yourself.

This made me better at CS, there are some slight bugs like how if you restart a map it might end up winning you the first round. Genuinely amazing to train though, the fundamentals haven't changed much from 1.6 to 2. 
Will edit once I've finished the Expert campaign since all I've finished is the normal campaign :)

Surprisingly fun single-player missions. Part of the fun in this game is just dealing with your incompetent bot teammates who don't always behave... properly. Aside from the main campaign provided with the game, there are plenty of third-party mission packs out there that you can install, and many of those are fantastic as well. I got a remarkable amount of enjoyment out of this game, despite its age.

Also, Turtle Rock rules! (Particularly Mike Booth. He's the guy responsible for most of the programming behind Valve's bot systems used in CS:CZ/CS:S/CS:GO as well as L4D/L4D2/TF2. That guy is awesome.)

I think its wrong to say that Condition Zero is the worst CS, because it's still 1.6 at heart if yall know what i mean. But it was quite disappointing, because Valve promised many new weapons, maps and even new classes in various interviews between 2001 and 2004. There were also screenshots and various videos of those maps, which i guess looked quite good of which only a few were included in the final product. And whats worse is since Source was released the same year as Condition Zero, it destroyed CZ completely and nobody cared about CZ anymore. CS Source came out which is another reason it got killed.
